documents.title: Setting Expectations and AI Policy
tiers: Use freely permitted with no acknowledgement
documents.summary: Teaching-center guidance telling instructors to define acceptable AI use, require attribution, explain ethics, state consequences and invite questions, with sample syllabus wording. It notes AI checkers are unreliable and explains that SCAI treats AI misuse as cheating or plagiarism according to each instructor's syllabus policy.
documents.stance_why: The page sets no rule of its own: it tells instructors to 'Clearly Define Acceptable AI Usage' in their syllabus and lists four approaches (prohibited, freely permitted, prior permission, with acknowledgment) that 'can be taken as is or combined', and SCAI judges cases 'based on the reporting professor's AI syllabus policy'. That hands the decision to instructors, so delegates with tiers.

units.why: The page tells instructors to specify which AI tools are 'permitted for assignments, projects, or examinations' and how; a requirement to state expectations, so the syllabus-statement type P09, addressed to instructors before the course.
units.anchor: specifying which AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT, Grammarly, AI-driven research assistants) are permitted
units.policy: Instructors specify which AI tools are permitted for assignments, projects, or examinations, and clearly state how they should or should not be used.

units.why: The guidance says the instructor 'may explicitly allow AI' for research, brainstorming or clarity while restricting it for critical analysis; the rule is set per instructor, so P04 rather than P15, which is the student-facing brainstorming allowance.
units.anchor: you may explicitly allow AI for preliminary research, brainstorming, or improving clarity in writing

units.why: The sample language permits ChatGPT for 'initial idea generation and clarifying concepts', a narrow allowed use; P15 (brainstorming) fits better than the tutor type P12 because idea generation is named first.
units.anchor: AI tools such as ChatGPT may be used for initial idea generation and clarifying concepts
units.frag_end: unless explicitly permitted by the instructor.

units.why: The sample says 'direct use of AI-generated content as your own analytical or creative work is strictly prohibited', which bars having AI produce submitted work (P19).
units.anchor: direct use of AI-generated content as your own analytical or creative work is strictly prohibited
units.frag_end: unless explicitly permitted by the instructor.

units.why: The sample lets the instructor lift the ban: 'unless explicitly permitted by the instructor' makes the rule depend on the instructor, so P04.
units.anchor: unless explicitly permitted by the instructor
units.frag_end: unless explicitly permitted by the instructor.
units.policy: AI-generated content may be used as the student's own analytical or creative work only if the instructor explicitly permits it.

units.why: Instructors are to explain that AI tools 'must be transparently acknowledged', a per-submission disclosure requirement (P24).
units.anchor: the use of AI tools must be transparently acknowledged
units.frag_end: correct citation formats for AI-generated content.

units.why: Instructors are told to 'Offer students explicit examples of correct citation formats for AI-generated content'; about how to cite but names no tool or prompt details, so P24 not P25.
units.anchor: Offer students explicit examples of correct citation formats for AI-generated content.
units.frag_end: correct citation formats for AI-generated content.

units.why: The sample syllabus language requires that AI-assisted ideas or text 'must be clearly cited in your submissions', a per-submission disclosure rule (P24).
units.anchor: must be clearly cited in your submissions
units.policy: Any ideas, concepts, or text developed with the assistance of an AI tool must be clearly cited in submissions.

units.why: The sample says failure to attribute 'will be considered plagiarism and may result in academic penalties', making nondisclosure itself the violation (P28); P36 also applies but P28 is the more specific rule.
units.anchor: Failure to attribute AI-generated content appropriately will be considered plagiarism

units.why: Instructors are told to 'Highlight ethical responsibilities' including bias and misrepresentation; an ethical-concerns statement, P53.
units.anchor: Highlight ethical responsibilities related to AI use, emphasizing transparency, fairness, and avoidance of bias

units.why: The sample says students 'are expected to critically reflect on the ethical implications of using AI' (bias, privacy, fairness); ethics concern, P53.
units.anchor: students are expected to critically reflect on the ethical implications of using AI

units.why: Instructors should 'Clearly outline the consequences for violating the course's AI policy'; stating penalties in advance, P37.
units.anchor: Clearly outline the consequences for violating the course’s AI policy

units.why: The sample classifies unauthorized use on assessments, failure to cite and submitting fully AI-generated work as 'violations of academic integrity policies', a misconduct classification (P36).
units.anchor: will be treated as violations of academic integrity policies
units.policy: Misuse of AI tools, such as unauthorized use on assessments, failure to cite appropriately, or submission of fully AI-generated work as your own, is treated as a violation of academic integrity policies, potentially leading to disciplinary action.

units.anchor: please reach out to me directly for clarification

units.frag_end: throughout the rest of the term.
units.policy: Instructors discuss the AI syllabus policy with students on the first day and again as a reminder throughout the term.

documents.title: Sample Language - Use of AI
tiers: General academic integrity statement including AI
documents.summary: A short page of sample syllabus language on AI from a crowd-sourced list. It offers five wordings from open encouragement to prohibition, with citation, permission and 25% cap variants.
documents.stance_why: It is a menu of sample syllabus statements ('Some Syllabus Language Samples') ranging from encouraging use to prohibiting it ('AI-generated submissions are not permitted'), so no single stance applies and the choice is left to instructors; delegates with tiers.

units.anchor: AI contributions must be attributed and true

units.anchor: The use of AI tools should be open and documented.

documents.title: Guidelines for the Effective and Responsible Use of AI in Dissertations
documents.summary: University Graduate School guidelines for AI in theses, dissertations and proposals. They set roles for students, mentors, programs and UGS, list acceptable and unacceptable uses, require disclosure in preliminary pages, limit detector use, and cover risks, privacy and a sample dissertation syllabus.
